titles.353: Annotatio I §.V open: Lutherans exclude only the tropus that exterminates substance — Bucer & Chytraeus
titles.354: Annotatio I §.V: Bucer — Luther rejected our reading as if it removed presence; nostri deny absence-sign
titles.355: Annotatio I §.V: Augustine’s signum corporis; contention de verbis not de re — Epist. Buceri ad Pontanum
titles.356: Annotatio I §.V: Calixtus Senior — Reformed metonymy as admissible ecclesiastical phrase
titles.357: Annotatio I §.V: Hoc pacto the controversy vanishes — tropus that keeps presence vs tropus that ejects it
titles.358: Annotatio I §.V close: Morton’s figurative proofs vs Pontificii — stop before Annotatio II

latin.353: His omnibus altius pensitatis, Lutherani ipsimet, nec alia mente tropum, nec alium tropum quemcunque, propositione Christi exclusum, cupiunt, quàm eâ mente sola, solumque illum tropum, qui corporis Christi veram substantiam Eucharistia exterminat, attestante illud prolixius Bucero, Oper. Anglican. pag. 704. num. 26. itemque apud Chytraeum pag. 660. in med.
latin.354: Quòd verò Lutherus, inquit, nostrorum interpretationem rejecit, ex eo, quantum ego quidem ex scriptis ejus judicare possum, factum est, quòd praesentiam Christi per eam in Coena tolli & removeri fuit arbitratus. Nostri vero panem ejusmodi signum corporis Christi nequaquam esse dicunt, per quod corpus Christi abesse vel non sumi denotetur, id quod multis scriptis editis hactenus notum fecerunt.
latin.355: Deinde & hoc manifestum est ex hac locutione, qua panis figura & signum corporis Christi esse dicitur, nequaquam sequi quòd corpus Christi propterea non adsit: aliàs enim de Augustino quoque dici posset, quòd nudum panem in Coena esse senserit, cum tamen contraria sententia in libris ipsius ubique reperiatur: nam contra Adamantum scribens his verbis usus est: Christus non dubitavit dicere, hoc est corpus meum, cùm daret signum corporis sui. Cùm igitur nostrae partis Doctores per interpretationem suam Christi praesentiam tollere aut negare nequaquam voluerint, sed in omnibus scriptis & libris suis eam sint testati, nec aliud quidpiam quam hoc planum facere & obtinere interpretatione sua studuerint, quòd panis non sit substantialiter corpus Christi, hac ratione vulgum à pane visibili ad Christum invisibilem adducere volentes, equidem non de re, sed tantum de verbis contentiones esse reperio. Epist. Buceri ad Pontanum non procul ab initio.
latin.356: Idem prorsus videtur Calixtus Senior innuere Judicio de controversiis num. 81. pag. m. 136., metonymicam Reformatorum propositionem ibidem Ecclesiasticam phrasin appellando quae admitti posset.
latin.357: Hoc verò pacto Controversia tota cessat omnino & evanescit, Reformatis tropum quidem defendentibus, sed qui corpus Christi Coenâ abesse haud patitur, nedum facit; Lutheranis verò tropo adversantibus, qui corpus Christi Coenâ movere ejusque praesentiam ex ea tollere minus verecundatur.
latin.358: Quod reliquum est, sensum verborum institutionis figurativum variis modis contra Pontificios probatum videas apud Mortonum, Episc. quondam Dunelmensem de Eucharistia, parte secunda Classe 1. cap. 2. 3. & 4.

pass_a.353: All these things having been weighed more deeply, the Lutherans themselves desire neither a tropus in another mind, nor any other tropus whatsoever, to be excluded from Christ’s proposition, than in that mind alone, and only that tropus which exterminates the true substance of Christ’s body from the Eucharist — Bucer attesting that at length (Opera Anglicana p. 704 no. 26), and likewise in Chytraeus p. 660 in the middle.
pass_a.354: But that Luther, he says, rejected our people’s interpretation — so far as I can judge from his writings — came about because he judged that by it Christ’s presence in the Supper was taken away and removed. Our people, however, by no means say that the bread is that kind of sign of Christ’s body by which Christ’s body is denoted to be absent or not taken — which they have made known hitherto by many published writings.
pass_a.355: Then this too is manifest from that locution by which the bread is said to be a figure and sign of Christ’s body: it by no means follows that Christ’s body is therefore not present — otherwise one could also say of Augustine that he sensed bare bread in the Supper, though the contrary opinion is found everywhere in his books: for writing against Adamantus he used these words: Christ did not hesitate to say, this is my body, when He was giving the sign of His body. Since therefore our side’s Doctors by their interpretation by no means wished to take away or deny Christ’s presence, but in all their writings and books have attested it, and have studied by their interpretation to make plain and obtain nothing other than this — that the bread is not substantially Christ’s body, wanting by this reason to lead the crowd from the visible bread to the invisible Christ — I indeed find the contentions to be not about the thing, but only about the words. Bucer’s Letter to Pontanus not far from the beginning.
pass_a.356: Calixtus Senior seems to hint the very same in Judgment on the Controversies no. 81, p. m. 136., there calling the Reformers’ metonymic proposition an Ecclesiastical phrase which could be admitted.
pass_a.357: But by this pact the whole Controversy ceases entirely and vanishes — the Reformed defending a tropus indeed, but one that by no means suffers Christ’s body to be absent from the Supper, still less makes it so; the Lutherans on the other hand opposing a tropus that is less ashamed to move Christ’s body from the Supper and take His presence out of it.
pass_a.358: As for what remains, see the figurative sense of the Institution words proved in various ways against the Pontificians in Morton, sometime Bishop of Durham, On the Eucharist, part two Class 1 chapters 2, 3, and 4.

353: Weighed more deeply: the Lutherans themselves want only one tropus shut out of This is my body — the kind that drives Christ’s true substance out of the Eucharist.
Bucer (Opera Anglicana p. 704 §26) and Chytraeus (p. 660 mid) attest that limit at length.
354: Bucer: Luther rejected our interpretation, so far as his writings show, because he thought it removed Christ’s presence from the Supper.
Our doctors deny that bread is a sign meaning the body is absent or not taken — and they have said so in many books.
355: Calling bread a figure and sign of Christ’s body does not prove the body is absent — else Augustine too would be read as teaching bare bread, though he wrote against Adamantus: Christ did not hesitate to say this is my body when giving the sign of His body.

Our doctors never meant to deny presence; they only press that bread is not substantially the body, to lead people from visible bread to invisible Christ — so the fight is about words, not the thing (Bucer to Pontanus).
356: Calixtus Senior points the same way (Judgment on the Controversies §81, p. 136): the Reformers’ metonymic proposition is an ecclesiastical phrase that could be admitted.
357: On that pact the whole controversy ceases and vanishes.

The Reformed defend a tropus that will not let Christ’s body be absent from the Supper — still less make it so; the Lutherans fight a tropus that is less shy about moving the body out and stripping presence from the meal.
358: For the rest, see Morton (sometime Bishop of Durham), On the Eucharist II Class 1 chs. 2–4, for figurative Institution proofs against the Pontificians.
